title: Permaculture

definition.text: An approach to designing land use and settlements that copies the arrangements found in thriving natural ecosystems.

facts.text: It rests on design principles drawn from whole-systems thinking, applied to farming, town planning, rewilding and community resilience.
Bill Mollison and David Holmgren coined the term in 1978, in opposition to industrial farming methods.
Earlier ideas of permanent agriculture, such as F. H. King's 1911 book and J. Russell Smith's Tree Crops of 1929, inspired it.
Holmgren set out twelve design principles, such as observe and interact, catch and store energy, and obtain a yield.
It favours perennial crops that need no yearly tilling and planting.
Critics say it is loosely defined and largely isolated from scientific literature.

contested_note: Critics argue permaculture lacks a clear definition and a scientific basis.

definition.text: The three core ethics of permaculture: care of the Earth, care of people, and setting limits to consumption and sharing the surplus.

facts.text: Mollison formulated them in 1988; Holmgren restated the third in 2002 as setting limits to consumption and reproduction and redistributing surplus.

definition.text: A layout that places parts of a design by how often people use them, numbered 0 to 5 outward from the house.

facts.text: Elements tended or harvested often go close to the house in zones 1 and 2; those used less are farther out.

definition.text: A mutually beneficial group of species that each provide different services within a larger ecosystem.

facts.text: Guild plants may supply food, draw up deep nutrients, fix nitrogen, attract helpful insects or repel pests.

definition.text: Burying wood in mounds or beds so that it soaks up water and keeps the soil moist.

facts.text: Enough buried wood can hold rainy-season water to carry crops through the dry season.

definition.text: Layering materials such as leaves, cardboard and wood chips over soil to imitate a forest floor.

facts.text: Mulch absorbs rain, cuts evaporation, adds organic matter, suppresses weeds and reduces erosion.
It is also used in regenerative agriculture to smother weeds and feed the soil.

definition.text: Collecting and storing rainwater for later use before it runs off or soaks into the ground.

facts.text: It supplies drinking water, livestock water and irrigation, and roof collection can significantly add to drinking water supply.

title: Rotational grazing

definition.text: Moving livestock between sections of pasture, called paddocks, so that the rest of the pasture can recover.

facts.text: It usually yields less than intensive livestock operations but needs fewer inputs, so net income per animal can be higher.
Each cow produces less, but more cows can graze each acre, giving more output per acre at less cost.
Pastures under some rotational systems erode less, and it may reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Manure returns most nutrients to the pasture, and swards with over 40% legumes need no commercial nitrogen.
Grazing animals on young legume-rich pasture risks bloat, which can be fatal.
In 87% of experiments, plant production was equal or greater under continuous grazing.
Virtual fencing with GPS collars can automate rotations.

contested_note: Scientists dispute whether rotational grazing beats continuous grazing for ecological goals; results depend on the management model.
